newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Indictments said possible in Israel corruption case.
newsitem.headline: Indictments said possible in Israel corruption case.

text.p: Israel's state prosecutor scrambled on Friday to counter a barrage of leaks to the media that police probing alleged government corruption were likely to issue criminal indictments against top officials.
The media reports renewed speculation Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government could topple over an ill-fated appointment of Jerusalem lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney general.
"It is too early to talk about the issuing of indictments," State Prosecutor Edna Arbel and Attorney General Elyakim Rubenstein said in a joint statement.
"The attorney general and the state prosecutor regret any inappropriate and unfounded publication during an investigation as sensitive as this."
The statement followed media reports that police would wrap up their probe of Bar-On's short-lived appointment last month with a flurry of criminal charge sheets.

Israeli press, radio and television were swamped with reports that police intended to indict Justice Minister Tsahi Hanegbi, Shas party leader Aryeh Deri and Netanyahu's aide Avigdor Lieberman in the affair.

All have denied any wrongdoing in the appointment of Bar-On, an activist in Netanyahu's Likud party. Bar-On resigned less than one day after taking office under criticism he was a legal lightweight unfit for the post.
A Channel One television report then alleged in January that the appointment not only reeked of routine back-room politics but was in fact criminal.

The television said that Deri, a kingmaker in Netanyahu's coalition on trial for the last three years for corruption, coerced the government to appoint Bar-On in the hopes of winning a plea bargain. Police immediately launched the investigation.
Legal experts say that Deri, Lieberman and Hanegbi could face charges of fraud, conspiracy and breach of public trust.
Some Israeli ministers have said that the government would collapse if the allegations proved true.
"I have said before that if this thing reaches the leadership ... the government will have to be sent home," Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told Israel radio.
The affair spilled across regional borders to Jordan. King Hussein said he believed Netanyahu would escape unscathed.

"Personally, I don't think that change will occur," King Hussein said in an interview with Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper published on Friday. "I hope we'll have stability in the region," he added.
The Israeli cabinet was forced to take up the affair in its weekly meeting on Friday, with some members blasting police for leaking the reports in order to influence the outcome of the investigation.
"Ministers criticised the leaks from the police concerning the ongoing investigation over the appointment," a cabinet statement said but did not elaborate.
But Kahalani charged that attacks on the police were a ploy by politicians to intimidate police investigators.
"Whoever tries to attack the investigative team in my opinion is diverting the investigation from its path," Kahalani told Israel radio after the cabinet meeting.
